title: Was There a Q?
subtitle: How Matthew, Mark and Luke are related: the data, the hypotheses, the arguments
lede: Matthew, Mark and Luke tell much of the same story in the same order and often in the same Greek words, so somebody copied somebody. Most scholars hold that Matthew and Luke each used Mark and a lost collection of sayings called Q. A substantial minority, whose leading voice is Mark Goodacre, holds that Luke used Matthew as well as Mark and that Q never existed; others do without Q by having Matthew use Luke, or Mark use both. This page sets out the evidence and every main argument on each side, with the replies, so the reasoning can be followed step by step.

sides.label: A lost source
sides.name: Q
sides.gloss: Matthew and Luke never saw each other's work. What they share beyond Mark, about 230 verses and mostly sayings of Jesus, comes from a written source that has not survived.
sides.heldBy: The majority since the 1860s: Holtzmann, Streeter, Kloppenborg, Tuckett

sides.label: No lost source
sides.name: Luke read Matthew
sides.gloss: Luke had Matthew's Gospel as well as Mark's. What Matthew and Luke share beyond Mark is what Luke took from Matthew, and Q is not needed.
sides.heldBy: Farrer, Goulder, Goodacre, Watson, Eve. Others turn it round: Matthew read Luke
